concepts.title: Features, Labels, and the Learning Problem
concepts.description: Every machine learning model consumes numbers, not raw real-world things. A feature is a numeric property of an example, and a label is the answer a supervised model is trained to reproduce; getting this representation wrong sinks a project long before algorithm choice matters.
learningObjectives: Define 'feature' and 'label' precisely, and distinguish a single feature vector from a raw, unprocessed data record.
Explain why feature representation is usually a bigger lever on model quality than algorithm choice.
Identify the roles of the feature matrix X and label vector y in standard supervised-learning notation.
Explain what feature engineering means, with at least one concrete example of deriving a useful feature from a raw field.
Recognize data leakage from a feature list or dataset description, and explain why it produces deceptively good results that fail in production.

sections.heading: From Real-World Things to Numbers: What a Feature Is
sections.body:
Every machine learning model, no matter how sophisticated, ultimately consumes numbers: not sentences, not images, not database rows as such, but arrays of numbers. A **feature** is a single measured or derived numeric property of one example in your dataset: a house's square footage, a user's number of days since signup, a pixel's brightness, the frequency of a particular word in an email. A collection of features describing one example, in a fixed and consistent order, is called a **feature vector**, and stacking many examples' feature vectors on top of each other gives you the **feature matrix**, conventionally called `X`, with one row per example and one column per feature.

This 'everything becomes numbers' rule holds even for data that doesn't look numeric at all. Text gets converted into token counts, embeddings, or other numeric encodings before any model touches it; images are already, technically, grids of pixel intensity numbers; categorical fields like a US state or a product category get mapped to numbers via encoding schemes (one-hot vectors, ordinal integers, learned embeddings). None of this is a detail to skip: *how* you turn a thing into numbers, and which of its properties you keep as features, sets a ceiling on what a model can learn, often more than the choice of algorithm does.

```python
house = {"sqft": 1450, "bedrooms": 3, "age_years": 12, "zip_code": "94110"}

# A model can't consume this dict directly -- it needs a fixed-order numeric vector.
feature_vector = [house["sqft"], house["bedrooms"], house["age_years"]]
print(feature_vector)   # [1450, 3, 12]
```

Notice that `zip_code` was left out of this vector rather than used as-is. Feeding the raw string `"94110"` into an algorithm that expects numbers would either error out or, if cast to an integer, imply that zip code 94110 is somehow 'less than' 94112 in a way that matters for house pricing, which it doesn't. Not every raw field belongs in a feature vector unchanged; some need thought about representation first.

sections.heading: Labels: The Answer You're Teaching the Model to Produce
sections.body:
If features are the inputs you show a model, a **label** is the answer you want it to learn to produce: the target value paired with each example's feature vector, conventionally called `y`. A labeled dataset is a set of `(features, label)` pairs: `(X[0], y[0])`, `(X[1], y[1])`, and so on, where `X[i]` is one example's feature vector and `y[i]` is the correct answer for that specific example. Labels only exist in **supervised learning**, covered in the next concept, where a model is trained to predict `y` from `X`. Plenty of machine learning has no labels at all, which is why a label is a different kind of thing from a feature, not just another column that happens to be special.

The nature of the label determines what kind of supervised problem you have. If `y` is a continuous number (a house's sale price, a delivery's estimated arrival time), you have a **regression** problem. If `y` is one of a fixed set of categories (spam or not spam, which of five product categories an item belongs to), you have a **classification** problem. This distinction cascades into nearly every downstream choice: which loss function makes sense, which evaluation metrics are meaningful, and even which algorithms are applicable at all.

```python
# Regression: label is a continuous number
houses_X = [[1450, 3, 12], [900, 2, 40], [2100, 4, 3]]
houses_y = [615000, 340000, 890000]   # sale price in dollars

# Classification: label is one of a fixed set of categories
emails_X = [[0.02, 1, 0], [0.31, 0, 1]]
emails_y = ["not_spam", "spam"]
```

`y` almost always has to come from *somewhere*: historical records, human annotators, a business outcome that eventually became known. That provenance is where the leakage risk discussed later in this concept originates. A label isn't a free fact sitting alongside the features; it's frequently the result of a separate, later, or more expensive process, and conflating the two is one of the most common modeling mistakes.

sections.heading: Why Representation Usually Matters More Than Algorithm Choice
sections.body:
Given a fixed dataset, changing which features you feed a model usually moves its performance more than changing which algorithm you use. Algorithm choice still matters, but 'garbage in, garbage out' is a bigger risk in practice than a suboptimal algorithm. A classic example: a raw timestamp like `2024-03-09T14:32:00` is nearly useless to a simple model as-is, because the model has no way to discover on its own that '2pm on a weekday' and '2pm on a Saturday' might mean very different things for, say, predicting traffic or app usage. **Feature engineering** -- deriving new, more informative features from raw fields -- makes hidden structure available to even a simple model:

```python
from datetime import datetime

def engineer_time_features(timestamp_str):
    dt = datetime.fromisoformat(timestamp_str)
    return {
        "hour_of_day": dt.hour,
        "day_of_week": dt.weekday(),
        "is_weekend": 1 if dt.weekday() >= 5 else 0,
    }

print(engineer_time_features("2024-03-09T14:32:00"))
# {'hour_of_day': 14, 'day_of_week': 5, 'is_weekend': 1}
```

A plain linear model can now use `is_weekend` as a signal. It could never have derived that from the raw ISO timestamp string, because it has no mechanism for parsing dates; it only multiplies numbers by weights and adds them up. This is where deep learning earns its reputation: architectures that learn useful intermediate representations from comparatively raw input (pixels, tokens), given enough data, reduce the amount of manual feature engineering required, though they never eliminate it. For tabular business data in modest quantities, thoughtful hand-engineered features with a simple, well-understood model routinely beat a fancier model fed raw fields.

sections.heading: Data Leakage: When Your Features Secretly Contain the Label (or the Future)
sections.body:
**Data leakage** happens when a feature encodes the label or wouldn't be available at the moment you need to make a prediction. It is one of the most common and damaging mistakes in applied machine learning, because it doesn't look like a bug. A leaky model typically trains and validates beautifully, because the leaked information correlates almost perfectly with the label in your historical data. Then it fails, usually without any error, the moment it predicts on a new case in production, where that information isn't available yet.

Suppose you're predicting whether a loan will default, and one of your features is `was_reported_delinquent`, a flag set by the collections team *after* a loan has already gone bad. A model trained with this feature looks like an outstanding classifier, because the flag is set for nearly every loan that defaulted. But at the moment you need the prediction, when the loan is issued, the flag doesn't exist yet. The feature is a byproduct of the label, not a predictor of it.

A sneakier flavor is **temporal leakage**: using information from the future relative to the prediction point, even if it isn't derived from the label. Randomly shuffling a time-ordered dataset before splitting it into train and validation sets, for instance, can put March rows in training and February rows in validation, so the model has effectively seen the future of part of what it is validated on. Validation metrics inflate without any real generalization. A reliable check against both flavors is to ask, for every feature: *at the moment I need this prediction in the real system, would this value already be known?* If the answer is 'not yet' or 'only because it was derived from the outcome I'm trying to predict,' the feature has to go.

examples.title: Turning a Raw Record Into a Feature Vector
examples.code:
house = {"sqft": 1450, "bedrooms": 3, "age_years": 12, "zip_code": "94110"}

feature_names = ["sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]
feature_vector = [house[name] for name in feature_names]

print(feature_vector)   # [1450, 3, 12]
examples.explanation: Building the vector from a `feature_names` list, rather than calling `list(house.values())`, is a deliberate choice, not a style preference. A Python dict preserves insertion order, but that is not a *consistent* feature order across every record you will ever build a vector from. If one record was constructed with its keys in a different order (or is missing a key, or has an extra one), `.values()` produces a vector whose columns don't line up with the other records' vectors, and nothing raises an error. Naming the features in a fixed order and looking each one up by key guarantees column 0 means `sqft` for every row. That matters because the plain list of numbers carries no such meaning once it's handed to a model.

examples.title: A Ratio Feature a Linear Model Can't Derive on Its Own
examples.code:
records = [
    {"beds": 3, "sqft": 1450},
    {"beds": 1, "sqft": 1450},
]

for r in records:
    r["sqft_per_bedroom"] = r["sqft"] / r["beds"]

print(records)
# [{'beds': 3, 'sqft': 1450, 'sqft_per_bedroom': 483.33...},
#  {'beds': 1, 'sqft': 1450, 'sqft_per_bedroom': 1450.0}]
examples.explanation: A plain linear model computes a weighted sum of its input features. It can multiply `sqft` by one weight and `beds` by another and add them, but it has no way to represent 'sqft divided by beds' unless you hand it that ratio as its own feature. Two houses with identical square footage can differ a lot in livability depending on bedroom count, and `sqft_per_bedroom` makes that relationship visible to even the simplest model, instead of hoping it infers a division from two separate linear terms, which it cannot do. More flexible model families (decision trees, neural networks) can sometimes discover such interactions given enough data, but engineering the ones you already know are meaningful is usually cheaper, more reliable, and more interpretable than hoping a complex model rediscovers them.

examples.title: Spotting a Leaky Feature Before It Costs You
examples.explanation: `was_reported_delinquent` is set by a downstream collections process once a loan is already in serious trouble, so by the time it's true, the loan has for practical purposes already defaulted or is about to. Including it doesn't help the model predict default; it lets the model 'predict' default from a value that is itself a symptom of default, and that exists in the historical dataset only because the outcome already happened. A model trained on it will show very high training and validation accuracy, because in historical data the flag and the label are almost perfectly correlated. Then it will be nearly useless in production, because when a real prediction is needed the flag hasn't been set yet and is either missing or always false. The fix is to remove any feature that is only known after, or as a consequence of, the event you're trying to predict.

misconceptions.description: More features is always better, because the model can just learn to ignore the useless ones.
misconceptions.clarification: Irrelevant or noisy features add variance and increase overfitting risk, especially with a limited number of training examples: a model with enough capacity can fit patterns in pure noise columns unless something like regularization or feature selection discourages it. More features also means more compute, more chances for data leakage to sneak in, and a harder-to-debug system. Models don't automatically know which columns are useless; that has to be established through feature selection, regularization, or domain judgment.

misconceptions.description: The label is basically just another column in the dataset that happens to be the target -- it comes from the same place, at the same time, as everything else.
misconceptions.clarification: Labels frequently come from a different, slower, or more expensive process than the features: a human annotation pass, an outcome that only becomes known weeks or months later, a downstream system's verdict. Treating the label as 'just another column collected alongside the rest' is the mental model that leads to data leakage: pulling in a feature that was derived from, or only available after, the label itself. Unsupervised learning, covered next, has no label at all, which shows that 'label' is a distinct role in the problem setup, not an interchangeable column.
misconceptions.fact: Labels frequently come from a different, slower, or more expensive process than the features: a human annotation pass, an outcome that only becomes known weeks or months later, a downstream system's verdict.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what's dangerous about the result?
hints: list(dict.values()) returns values in whatever order the dict's keys were inserted -- is that order guaranteed to be the same for house_a and house_b?
Compare the key order of house_a and house_b line by line -- they're not written in the same order.
Think about what 'column 0 of the feature matrix' is supposed to mean across every row -- does it actually mean the same thing for both rows here?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints [[1200, 3, 10], [2, 900, 5]]. This is dangerous because column 0 is sqft for house_a's vector but bedrooms for house_b's vector: the values come out in whatever order each dict happened to be written, not in a consistent, chosen feature order.
exercises.solutionExplanation: house_a's keys are written sqft, bedrooms, age, so to_vector(house_a) is [1200, 3, 10]. house_b's keys are written bedrooms, sqft, age, so to_vector(house_b) is [2, 900, 5]. Both are valid Python lists of three numbers, so nothing crashes, but 'column 0' means sqft in the first row and bedroom count in the second, and any model fed this matrix would learn from a column that mixes two unrelated quantities. Relying on dict insertion order for feature order is this trap; the fix is to build every vector from a fixed list of feature names, looked up by key.

exercises.prompt: This feature-building function is meant to help predict whether a loan will default, but a data scientist reviewing it flagged it as broken before it ever reaches production. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: Ask, for each field, whether it would actually be known at the moment you need to make this prediction -- before you know if the loan will default.
'was_reported_delinquent' is set by a collections process -- when, relative to a loan actually defaulting, does that flag typically get turned on?
A feature that's really a downstream consequence of the label isn't a predictor of it -- it needs to be removed from the feature set entirely, not adjusted.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `was_reported_delinquent` is a leaky feature: a downstream collections process sets it once a loan is already in trouble, so it is almost a restatement of the label rather than an independent predictor, and it would not be available when a prediction is needed (when the loan is issued). Training with it would produce deceptively excellent validation metrics and a model that collapses in production, since the flag doesn't exist yet for a new loan. The fix is to remove it from the feature set, keeping only fields known at prediction time, like `amount`, `credit_score`, and `days_since_last_payment`.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following most directly describes 'data leakage' in a supervised learning context?
options: The label vector y has missing values for some rows.
A feature contains information that would not actually be available at the time you need to make a real prediction, or is derived from the label itself.
Using too many features, which slows down training.
The training set and test set were shuffled together before splitting.
assessments.explanation: Data leakage means a feature carries information that either encodes the label or wouldn't be available at prediction time, producing deceptively good training and validation results that don't hold up in production. The “Using too many features, which slows down training” option describes a cost/performance concern, not leakage. The “The label vector y has missing values…” option describes a missing-data problem, unrelated to leakage. The “The training set and test set were…” option describes a specific *cause* that can lead to temporal leakage in time-ordered data, but it's a narrower scenario than the general definition.

assessments.prompt: In the house example, the raw field zip_code (e.g. "94110") is left out of the feature vector rather than being cast to an integer. What is the danger of casting it?
options: Feature vectors are structurally unable to contain any value that was originally a string.
Converting a 5-digit string to an integer would consume too much memory for a typical model.
Casting it straight to a number would imply a false numeric relationship.
Zip codes change too frequently over time to be used as a feature at all.
assessments.explanation: Casting "94110" to an integer would imply that zip code 94110 is somehow 'less than' 94112 in a way that matters for house pricing, which isn't true: zip codes are categorical, not ordinal, even though they're written as digits. The “Converting a 5-digit string to an integer…” option invents a memory concern that has nothing to do with the issue. The “Zip codes change too frequently over time…” option is false: zip codes are fairly stable, and that isn't the reason. The “Feature vectors are structurally unable to contain…” option is wrong because strings routinely become features once encoded (one-hot, embeddings, etc.); the problem is that naive numeric casting creates a fake ordering, not that strings are unusable.

assessments.prompt: The concept adds a derived feature with `r["sqft_per_bedroom"] = r["sqft"] / r["beds"]` rather than just feeding `sqft` and `beds` separately into a plain linear model. Why does this matter specifically for a linear model?
options: A linear model computes a weighted sum of its inputs and has no built-in way to represent a division/interaction between two features unless that ratio is handed to it as its own explicit feature.
The ratio feature removes the need for a label vector y during training.

Dividing sqft by beds always produces a smaller number, which by itself makes training converge faster regardless of the model, and a linear model is the only kind of model whose training time depends on the size of its inputs.
Linear models can only accept a single numeric feature at a time, so beds and sqft cannot both be inputs.
assessments.explanation: A linear model can multiply sqft by one weight and beds by another and add them, but it has no way to represent 'sqft divided by beds' as a single quantity unless that ratio is provided as its own feature. More flexible models like trees or neural networks can sometimes discover such interactions automatically, but a plain linear model cannot. The “Linear models can only accept a single…” option is false -- linear models routinely take many features at once. The “Dividing sqft by beds always produces…” option makes a training-speed claim that isn't true. The “The ratio feature removes the need…” option confuses feature engineering with label removal; adding a derived feature has nothing to do with whether y is needed.

assessments.prompt: A team builds a fraud model by taking a full year of time-ordered transactions, randomly shuffling every row, and then splitting the shuffled data 80/20 into train and test sets. Based on the concept's discussion of leakage, what risk does this specific procedure create?
options: The resulting feature matrix X will have a different number of columns in train versus test.
None -- randomly shuffling rows before splitting is the standard, safe way to build a train/test split for any dataset.
Shuffling rows silently changes the numeric values stored inside each feature vector.

Temporal leakage: shuffling before splitting a time-ordered dataset can let the model trained on data from one period 'see' patterns from a period it's later validated against (or vice versa), inflating validation metrics in a way that doesn't reflect genuine generalization.
assessments.explanation: This failure mode is 'temporal leakage': randomly shuffling rows before splitting a time-ordered dataset can leak information across the boundary between train and validation periods, producing validation metrics that look good but don't reflect real-world generalization. The “None -- randomly shuffling rows before splitting…” option is the opposite of the right advice for time-ordered data. The “The resulting feature matrix X will have…” and “Shuffling rows silently changes the numeric values…” options describe mechanical impossibilities -- shuffling rows doesn't change column counts or the values inside any individual row, only their order.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who has just learned what features and labels are, why data leakage is such a dangerous bug in practice: why it's easy to introduce, why it's hard to catch just by looking at validation metrics, and how to guard against it.
assessments.modelAnswer: Data leakage happens when a feature secretly contains information that comes from the label itself or wouldn't exist yet at the moment you need a real prediction. It's easy to introduce because it doesn't look like a bug. It looks like a helpful, plausible column that happened to be sitting in the same table as everything else, like a 'was flagged for review' field that is only ever set after the bad outcome you're trying to predict has already happened. It's hard to catch from validation metrics because the leaked feature correlates almost perfectly with the label in historical data, which is why it leaks in the first place. Training and validation accuracy both look excellent, sometimes suspiciously so, and nothing signals a problem until the model is deployed against current data where that information isn't populated yet, and performance collapses. The most reliable guard is a feature-by-feature question: at the moment you'd need this prediction in the real system, would this value already be known, and is it independent of the outcome you're predicting, or a byproduct of it? A secondary guard is suspicion of validation performance that looks unusually close to perfect. Real-world signals are rarely that clean, and an almost-perfect score is often a leak rather than a triumph.

concepts.title: Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: The supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement split is about what training signal is available -- known labels, no labels at all, or a delayed reward -- and that signal, not the algorithm, defines the shape of the problem you're solving.
learningObjectives: Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning by what training signal is available, not by which algorithm is used.
Give a concrete example problem for each paradigm and explain specifically why it fits that category.
Explain the difference between classification and regression as sub-types of supervised learning.
Explain what a reward is in reinforcement learning and how it differs structurally from a label.
Explain why the same raw dataset can sometimes be approached from more than one paradigm depending on the question being asked.
Describe self-supervised learning and explain why it behaves like supervised learning despite requiring no human-annotated labels.

sections.heading: What Signal Do You Have?
sections.body:
The taxonomy of 'supervised,' 'unsupervised,' and 'reinforcement' learning is not about which algorithm you use. It's about what feedback signal is available while the model learns, and that signal shapes everything else about the problem. In **supervised learning**, you have a dataset of `(features, label)` pairs: for every example you know the correct answer, and training is a search for parameters that make predictions match those answers as closely as possible, on average. In **unsupervised learning**, you only have features, `X`, with no labels. There is no 'correct answer' to match against, so the model looks for structure in the data itself: groups of similar examples, a lower-dimensional way to represent the same information, patterns of what's 'typical' versus 'unusual.' In **reinforcement learning**, there's no dataset of pre-labeled correct answers. Instead, an agent takes actions inside an environment and receives a reward signal, often only after a whole sequence of actions, and has to learn, through trial and error, which actions tend to lead to good outcomes.

This framing matters because the same raw data can sometimes be approached from more than one paradigm, depending on the question you ask of it. A dataset of customer purchase histories could be used to build a supervised churn classifier (if you have historical labels for who actually churned), or fed into unsupervised clustering to discover customer segments nobody had names for yet, or even shape a reinforcement learning problem if you're deciding, sequentially, which offer to show a customer next and only find out much later whether that sequence of decisions paid off. The paradigm is a property of the *problem setup you choose*, not of the raw data sitting in a table.

sections.heading: Supervised Learning: Classification vs Regression
sections.body:
Within supervised learning, the type of label splits problems into two families you'll see referenced constantly. **Classification** problems have a label drawn from a fixed, finite set of categories -- spam or not spam, which of several product categories, whether a transaction is fraudulent. **Regression** problems have a label that's a continuous number -- a price, a temperature, a number of days until churn. This distinction determines which loss functions are even mathematically sensible (comparing 'how far' one category is from another rarely means anything, but subtracting two numbers always gives an error, which is why classification and regression use different loss functions, covered in the next concept), which evaluation metrics apply (precision/recall belong to classification; mean absolute error belongs to regression), and which algorithms apply, since some model families come in separate classification and regression variants despite confusingly similar names (logistic regression solves classification; linear regression solves regression).

A few edge cases will come up later: **ordinal regression** handles labels that are categories with a meaningful order (star ratings 1 through 5) using techniques that sit between plain classification and plain regression; **multi-label classification** allows an example to belong to more than one category at once (a news article tagged both 'politics' and 'technology'), unlike standard classification, where exactly one category applies. These aren't exotic; they show up constantly in product data. But get the classification-vs-regression split solid before layering these on.

sections.heading: Unsupervised Learning: Finding Structure Without Answers
sections.body:
Without labels to check against, unsupervised learning has to define success differently, and the definition depends on the sub-task. **Clustering** groups examples into subsets that are similar to each other and different from other groups -- algorithms like k-means look for group assignments that minimize the distance between each point and its group's center. There's no 'correct' group name, only relative similarity. **Dimensionality reduction** (like PCA) finds a smaller set of derived features that still capture most of the important variation in the original, larger feature set -- useful for visualization, compressing data before feeding it to another model, or removing redundant features. **Anomaly detection** learns what 'typical' data looks like and flags examples that deviate strongly from it, without being told in advance what an anomaly looks like.

The hard part of unsupervised learning, and the reason it's harder to evaluate than supervised learning, is that there usually is no ground truth to check your result against. If a clustering algorithm splits customers into four groups, there's no answer key to compare against the way you'd compare a classifier's predictions to known labels. You're left judging whether the groups are internally coherent, well separated, and useful for the downstream decision that motivated building them. That is why a metric like accuracy has no direct unsupervised equivalent.

sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning: Reward Instead of Right Answers
sections.body:
Reinforcement learning (RL) frames a problem as an **agent** interacting with an **environment** over a sequence of steps: at each step the agent observes some **state**, chooses an **action**, and receives a **reward** (a scalar number) along with a new state. There is no dataset of 'this state, this is the one correct action' pairs handed to the agent up front -- it has to discover, through its own trial and error across many episodes, which actions tend to lead to higher cumulative reward over time. This creates a different kind of problem, the **credit assignment problem**: if a reward only arrives at the very end of a long sequence of moves (win or lose a full game of chess, for instance), which of the dozens of moves along the way deserves credit or blame for that outcome? Supervised learning never has to answer this question, because every training example already comes with its own, immediate, unambiguous correct answer attached.

RL is easy to over-romanticize as the 'most advanced' paradigm, so it helps to be clear about when it's the right tool. It fits sequential decision-making problems where you don't have, and often can't get, a dataset of correct actions: game-playing, robotic control, resource allocation over time. But it is typically far less sample-efficient than supervised learning, often needing enormous numbers of trial-and-error interactions to learn anything useful, and considerably harder to debug, since there's no simple 'compare prediction to label' check at every step. If a problem has labeled correct answers available, supervised learning is almost always the simpler, cheaper, more reliable choice. Reach for RL when the problem is about a sequence of decisions with delayed, cumulative feedback and no supervision signal exists for any individual decision.

sections.heading: Where the Lines Blur: Self-Supervised Learning
sections.body:
One increasingly important pattern doesn't fit neatly into any of the three boxes above: **self-supervised learning**, where a model generates its own labels from unlabeled data by withholding part of the input and training itself to predict the withheld part. A common example: take a huge amount of raw, unlabeled text, hide the next word in a sentence, and train a model to predict it from everything before it -- the 'label' at each position is the next token in the original text, which required no human annotation, since the text already contained its own answer key. This is the core pretraining technique behind modern large language models. It looks unsupervised (no human ever attached a label) but is optimized exactly like supervised learning (there is a correct-answer label at every position, derived automatically from the data rather than annotated by a person).

Real systems frequently chain paradigms together rather than picking one: a large language model might be pretrained with self-supervised next-token prediction on massive unlabeled text, then fine-tuned with ordinary supervised learning on a smaller labeled dataset for a specific task, then further adjusted with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where human preferences between candidate outputs become the reward signal. None of this contradicts the three-paradigm framework; it's the same framework applied at different stages of one pipeline.

examples.title: Classification vs Regression: Same Shape, Different Label
examples.code:
# Regression: predicting a continuous price
house_features = [[1450, 3, 12], [900, 2, 40]]
house_price_labels = [615000.0, 340000.0]

# Classification: predicting one of a fixed set of categories
email_features = [[0.02, 1, 0], [0.31, 0, 1]]
email_category_labels = ["not_spam", "spam"]

# The feature matrices look identical in shape; only the TYPE of y differs.
examples.explanation: Nothing about the structure of `house_features` or `email_features` reveals whether you're looking at a regression or classification problem, since both are numeric matrices. The distinction lives in `y`: a continuous, ordered number for the house prices versus a value from a small, fixed, unordered set of strings for the email categories. This matters mechanically, not just semantically. A linear-regression-style model can't be fit against `email_category_labels` (what is an error between the string 'spam' and a numeric prediction?), and fitting a classifier against continuous prices would require bucketing prices into categories first, throwing away the ordering a regression model would use. Check what `y` is before choosing a model family; it's a five-second check that prevents a wrong approach.

examples.title: Unsupervised Clustering: fit(X) With No y at All
examples.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = [[1, 2], [1, 4], [10, 2], [10, 4]]

model = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0)
model.fit(X)          # note: no y argument anywhere -- there isn't one

print(model.labels_)   # e.g. [1 1 0 0] -- CLUSTER ids, not class names
examples.explanation: `KMeans.fit` takes only `X`; there's no label parameter, because unsupervised learning has no labels to give it. The `labels_` attribute it produces is easy to confuse with a classifier's predicted labels, but it means something different: arbitrary cluster identifiers, integers assigned in whatever order the algorithm happened to discover the groups, not predictions of any real-world category. There's no guarantee cluster 0 corresponds to anything a human would find meaningful, and running the algorithm again with a different `random_state` can flip which integer goes to which group of points even though the grouping stays the same. Evaluating a clustering result therefore can't use the 'does the predicted label match the true label' check a classifier's output can, a theme that returns in this concept's exercises.

examples.title: A Reinforcement Learning Loop, Skeleton
examples.code:
# fragment: assumes env, agent and max_steps are defined elsewhere
state = env.reset()
total_reward = 0

for step in range(max_steps):
    action = agent.choose_action(state)
    next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)

    agent.learn(state, action, reward, next_state)
    total_reward += reward
    state = next_state

    if done:
        break

print(f"Episode finished with total reward: {total_reward}")
examples.explanation: Compare this with a supervised training loop: there is no `y` anywhere, and no per-step 'correct action' to compare against. `agent.choose_action(state)` picks an action based on what the agent has learned so far, often with some randomness early on to keep exploring rather than always exploiting its current best guess. `env.step(action)` is the only place any feedback appears, as a scalar `reward` and a `next_state`, and that reward may be zero or near-meaningless for most steps, becoming informative only once accumulated across an episode. `agent.learn(...)` is where the parameter updates happen, using this reward instead of a label. It learns from one `(state, action, reward, next_state)` tuple at a time, with no way to know whether this particular action was the one responsible for whatever reward eventually arrived. That is the credit assignment problem in code.

misconceptions.description: Unsupervised learning is just supervised learning without labels -- same algorithms, just skip the y.
misconceptions.clarification: The two have different objectives, not just a missing argument. Supervised learning minimizes prediction error against a known ground truth; unsupervised learning optimizes a structural criterion (cluster compactness, reconstruction error, likelihood of the data under a model) that doesn't require agreement with any external answer, because there isn't one. In practice this leads to different algorithm families (k-means, PCA, and autoencoders for unsupervised tasks versus linear regression, logistic regression, and decision trees for supervised ones), even though a few techniques straddle the boundary.

misconceptions.description: Reinforcement learning is 'better' or more advanced than supervised learning, so it should be used whenever possible to get a 'smarter' model.
misconceptions.clarification: RL is suited to a specific problem shape, sequential decision-making with delayed rewards and no direct supervision signal for any individual action, rather than being a generally superior technique. It's typically far less sample-efficient and considerably harder to train and debug than supervised learning. If you have labeled correct answers for the thing you're trying to predict, supervised learning is almost always simpler, cheaper, and more reliable. Reaching for RL by default, when a supervised framing would work, adds cost and fragility without adding capability.
misconceptions.fact: RL is suited to a specific problem shape, sequential decision-making with delayed rewards and no direct supervision signal for any individual action, rather than being a generally superior technique.

exercises.prompt: What does model.labels_ contain after this runs, and why was y never used anywhere in the code even though it looks like a labeled classification problem?
exercises.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = [[1, 2], [1, 4], [10, 2], [10, 4]]
y = ["red", "red", "blue", "blue"]

model = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0)
model.fit(X)
print(model.labels_)
hints: Check the signature of KMeans().fit() -- does it accept a label argument at all, anywhere?
model.labels_ describes which group each point was assigned to, not which real-world category it belongs to -- those are two different things.
Since y is never passed into .fit(), it plays no part in the computation. It's an unused variable here.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints two cluster ids over the four points, something like [0, 0, 1, 1] or [1, 1, 0, 0] -- the integers depend on arbitrary internal ordering, not on the meaning of 'red'/'blue'. y is unused because KMeans.fit only accepts X; it is an unsupervised algorithm with no way to consume a label.
exercises.solutionExplanation: KMeans finds two groups of points that are close together -- here, clearly ({1,2},{1,4}) and ({10,2},{10,4}) -- and assigns each group an arbitrary integer id, stored in `labels_`. Because `y` is defined but never passed into `.fit()` or referenced again, it plays no role in the computation; the code would run identically if the `y = [...]` line were deleted. It's easy to see a variable named `y` next to the data and assume it's used the way it would be in a supervised classifier's `.fit(X, y)` call, but unsupervised APIs have no label parameter.

exercises.prompt: This code tries to check how well KMeans recovered the true 'red'/'blue' grouping by comparing predicted cluster ids to true labels directly, and reports 0% accuracy even though the clustering, inspected by eye, looks perfect. Explain what's wrong and fix the evaluation.
exercises.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import numpy as np

X = [[1, 2], [1, 4], [10, 2], [10, 4]]
y_true = [0, 0, 1, 1]

model = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0)
model.fit(X)
predicted = model.labels_

accuracy = np.mean(predicted == y_true)
print(accuracy)  # prints 0.0
hints: Print `predicted` and `y_true` side by side -- are the two GROUPINGS the same, even if the specific numbers used to label each group differ?
KMeans has no idea that '0' should mean the same thing as whatever '0' means in y_true -- cluster index numbering is arbitrary and unrelated to any external label's numbering.

You need a comparison that's invariant to which specific integer got assigned to which group -- either match clusters to the majority true label first, or use a permutation-invariant clustering metric like adjusted_rand_score.
exercises.solutionCode:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

X = [[1, 2], [1, 4], [10, 2], [10, 4]]
y_true = [0, 0, 1, 1]

model = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0)
model.fit(X)
predicted = model.labels_

score = adjusted_rand_score(y_true, predicted)
print(score)  # 1.0 -- the grouping is actually perfect
exercises.solutionExplanation: The clustering itself is perfect: the two groups ({1,2},{1,4}) and ({10,2},{10,4}) are recovered, but with this seed KMeans numbered them the opposite way from `y_true` (its cluster '0' corresponds to y_true's '1', and vice versa). Comparing `predicted == y_true` element-wise checks for numeric agreement, which fails completely under this swap even though the grouping is identical, giving a misleading 0.0. `adjusted_rand_score` (and similar clustering metrics) checks whether two groupings agree on *which points are grouped together*, regardless of which integer got attached to each group. That is the comparison that makes sense for unsupervised output, since cluster ids have no inherent mapping to any external label space. (Which integers KMeans picks can differ between seeds and library versions, so run it and check that `predicted` really is swapped.)

assessments.prompt: A model is trained on years of chess game logs, receiving a win/loss outcome only at the end of each full game, and must learn a sequence of moves that leads to winning. Which learning paradigm best fits this setup, and why?
options: It's not a machine learning problem at all, since chess has fixed rules.
Unsupervised learning, because there's no explicit right answer for any individual move.
Supervised learning, because each move can be labeled correct or incorrect from the game record, so an ordinary classifier can be trained on those labels one move at a time.
Reinforcement learning, because the feedback is a delayed scalar reward tied to a whole sequence of actions, not a per-action label.
assessments.explanation: This is the reinforcement learning shape: an agent (the chess player) takes a sequence of actions (moves) in an environment (the game) and receives a reward (win/loss) only after the full sequence, which raises the credit-assignment problem of working out which moves mattered. The “Supervised learning, because each move can…” option is wrong because no individual move in the historical logs comes with its own 'correct move' label -- only the final outcome is known. The “Unsupervised learning, because there's no explicit right…” option is wrong because the problem does have a feedback signal (win/loss); it's delayed and sequence-level, not absent, which differs from the unsupervised setting. The “It's not a machine learning problem…” option is wrong because fixed rules don't prevent a decision-making problem from being learned: they define the environment, not whether learning applies to it.

assessments.prompt: Self-supervised learning (e.g. hiding the next word in a sentence and training a model to predict it from everything before it) looks unsupervised but behaves like supervised learning. Why?
options: Because the 'label' at each position is the actual next token already present in the raw text.
Because self-supervised systems still require a scalar reward signal from an environment, just like reinforcement learning.
Because it always uses neural networks, and neural networks are inherently a supervised technique.
Because it groups similar sentences together with no target value of any kind, exactly like clustering.
assessments.explanation: Self-supervised learning looks unsupervised because no human ever attached a label, but it is optimized like supervised learning because there is a correct-answer label at every position, derived automatically from the data (the next token) instead of hand-annotated. The “Because it always uses neural networks…” option is false; the technique isn't tied to any one algorithm family. The “Because self-supervised systems still require a scalar…” option describes reinforcement learning's reward signal, not self-supervised learning's label. The “Because it groups similar sentences together…” option describes unsupervised clustering, the opposite of what makes self-supervised learning behave like supervised learning.

assessments.prompt: The concept says unsupervised learning is 'meaningfully harder to evaluate' than supervised learning. What is the core reason given for this?
options: Unsupervised algorithms are always much slower to run than supervised ones, making evaluation impractical.

There is usually no ground truth to check the result against, so you're left judging whether the discovered structure is internally coherent and actually useful, not comparing predictions to known correct answers.
Unsupervised learning can only be applied to image data, which is hard to inspect visually.
Unsupervised algorithms never produce a stable, repeatable result across runs.
assessments.explanation: With clustering, for instance, there's no answer key to compare against the way you'd compare a classifier's predictions to known labels. You instead evaluate coherence, separation, and usefulness for the downstream decision, which is why accuracy-style metrics have no direct unsupervised equivalent. The “Unsupervised algorithms are always much slower…”, “Unsupervised learning can only be applied…”, and “Unsupervised algorithms never produce a stable, repeatable…” options are all unsupported claims and are not generally true of unsupervised methods.

assessments.prompt: In reinforcement learning, which challenge does the term 'credit assignment problem' refer to?
options: Deciding how much compute budget should be allocated to training the agent.
Splitting a labeled dataset fairly between the training and validation sets.
Figuring out which of the many actions taken earlier in a sequence actually deserves credit or blame for a reward that only arrives at the very end of that sequence.
Assigning a numeric probability to every possible action before the agent chooses one.
assessments.explanation: Chess shows the credit assignment problem: if a reward only arrives at the very end of a long sequence of moves, which of the dozens of moves along the way deserves credit or blame for that outcome? Supervised learning never faces this because every example already comes with its own immediate, unambiguous label. The “Deciding how much compute budget should…”, “Assigning a numeric probability to every possible…”, and “Splitting a labeled dataset fairly between…” options describe unrelated concerns (compute budgeting, action-probability estimation, and dataset splitting) that this term doesn't name.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague, using the training signal (not the algorithm) as the organizing idea, how supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning differ, and why the same real dataset could sometimes be used in more than one paradigm depending on what question you ask of it.
assessments.modelAnswer: The cleanest way to tell these apart is to ask what feedback the learning process has access to, not which algorithm gets used. Supervised learning has examples that come with the correct answer attached: every training example is a (features, label) pair, and training is a search for parameters that make predictions match those answers as closely as possible. Unsupervised learning has only the features, with no correct answer for anything, so it defines success from structure in the data itself (how tightly points cluster together, how well a compressed representation reconstructs the original) rather than matching against ground truth. Reinforcement learning has neither a labeled dataset nor a structural criterion over static data. An agent takes actions in an environment and receives a reward signal, often only after a whole sequence of decisions, and learns by trial and error which actions tend to lead to good long-run outcomes, without ever being told the correct action for any single step. Because the taxonomy is about the *signal available*, not a property fixed to the raw data, the same dataset can support more than one framing: a table of customer purchase histories could train a supervised churn classifier if you have historical churn labels, feed unsupervised clustering to find customer segments if you ignore or don't have those labels, or underlie a reinforcement learning setup if the question is a sequence of marketing decisions evaluated only by their eventual cumulative effect. The paradigm follows from the question being asked of the data.

concepts.title: The Train/Predict Loop and Loss Functions
concepts.description: A model is a parameterized function; a loss function turns 'how wrong was this prediction' into a single number to minimize; and 'learning' mechanically means searching for parameter values that make that number small, nothing more mystical than that.
learningObjectives: Describe a model as a parameterized function f(x; theta) and explain what training changes versus what stays fixed at prediction time.
Explain the difference between the train step and the predict/inference step, and why production systems normally run only the predict step.
Define a loss function and explain why it must reduce a prediction/label comparison to a single scalar number.
Compute mean squared error by hand for a small example.
Explain why 'learning' mechanically means searching for parameter values that minimize average loss over training data, not something resembling human understanding.
Distinguish the loss used to optimize a model from the evaluation metric used to judge and report it.

sections.heading: A Model Is Just a Parameterized Function
sections.body:
Strip away the terminology, and a trained model is a function: `y_hat = f(x; theta)`, where `x` is a feature vector, `y_hat` is the prediction, and `theta` is a set of numeric **parameters** the function depends on. The *form* of `f` (a linear combination, a stack of neural network layers) is chosen ahead of time by whoever designed the architecture, and it generally does not change during training. (Decision trees are a partial exception: their structure is itself learned from the data.) What training searches over is `theta`: the numeric values plugged into that fixed form. For an ordinary linear model with two features, that is simple: `y_hat = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b`, and `theta = (w1, w2, b)`, three plain numbers.

```python
def predict(x1, x2, w1, w2, b):
    return w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + b

# Before training: parameters are arbitrary (often zero or small random values)
print(predict(1450, 3, w1=0.0, w2=0.0, b=0.0))     # 0.0 -- useless

# After training: parameters have been adjusted to fit real data
print(predict(1450, 3, w1=210.0, w2=15000.0, b=50000.0))   # a real-looking price
```

The function `predict` never changes between these two calls: not one character of its code is different. Only the numbers passed in for `w1`, `w2`, and `b` changed. Mechanically, that is what training does: it finds good numbers for a function whose shape was already decided.

sections.heading: Loss: Turning 'Wrong' Into a Number You Can Optimize
sections.body:
A **loss function** takes one prediction and the corresponding true label and produces a single non-negative number describing how wrong that particular prediction was -- zero, or close to it, for a great prediction; larger for a worse one. For regression, the most common choice is **mean squared error (MSE)**: square the difference between prediction and label, so errors in either direction count as positive and larger errors are penalized disproportionately more than smaller ones, then average across every example in the batch or dataset being measured.

```python
def mse(y_true, y_pred):
    n = len(y_true)
    squared_errors = [(yt - yp) ** 2 for yt, yp in zip(y_true, y_pred)]
    return sum(squared_errors) / n

print(mse(y_true=[100, 200, 300], y_pred=[110, 190, 305]))   # a small positive number
```

For classification, squaring a difference between predicted and true *category* doesn't mean anything -- there's no meaningful arithmetic distance between 'spam' and 'not spam' -- so classification typically uses **cross-entropy loss** instead, which compares a predicted probability for each class against the true class and penalizes confident wrong predictions especially heavily. The formula matters less here than the idea both losses share: a loss function is a mathematical, usually differentiable, stand-in for 'wrongness,' chosen so an optimization procedure can use it as a target to minimize. What you train against is not the loss on one example but the **average loss across the whole training set** (or a batch of it). That average is usually what people mean by 'the loss' or 'the cost function' in a training run.

sections.heading: The Train Step vs. The Predict Step
sections.body:
Two different operations involve the same function `f(x; theta)`, and conflating them is a source of production bugs. The **train step** consumes `(X, y)` pairs -- both features and true labels -- and produces or updates `theta`, typically by looping over the training data many times (each full pass is an **epoch**) and nudging `theta` after each look at the data, using the loss as a guide (the mechanics of that nudging, gradient descent, are the subject of the next module). The **predict step**, also called **inference**, consumes only `X` and produces `y_hat = f(x; theta)`, using whatever `theta` training already settled on; it does not need or use `y`, because in a real deployment the point is to predict an outcome you don't know yet.

In practice, once training is finished, the artifact you deploy to production is the learned `theta` values plus the fixed architecture, serialized to disk: a file of numbers. Serving predictions means loading that file and repeatedly running the predict step on new incoming `X`, with no further training by default (systems that keep learning after deployment, called online learning, are a more advanced design choice). A trap follows from this. Batch scoring pipelines sometimes join in a ground-truth outcome column for convenience or monitoring, and if that column ever gets used as a feature during prediction, rather than kept separate for later evaluation, you've reintroduced the data leakage problem from the earlier concept, now at serving time instead of training time. That is often harder to notice, because it doesn't show up until you inspect the feature list line by line.

sections.heading: What 'Learning' Mechanically Means
sections.body:
Put the previous three sections together and 'a model learns' has a plain mechanical meaning: an iterative search procedure looks at training examples, computes how wrong the current `theta` makes the model's predictions (the loss), and adjusts `theta` in a way that tends to make that loss smaller, repeating this many times until the loss stops improving by much. Nothing in that loop requires understanding in a human sense. It's numerical optimization of a scalar function, and no less useful for being 'just' that.

A naive version of this loop, using random nudges instead of calculus, shows the mechanics without needing derivatives. Real systems use a smarter version of the idea, gradient descent, covered in the next module:

```python
# uses mse() as defined above
import random

def predict(x, w, b):
    return w * x + b

x_data = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y_data = [3, 5, 7, 9]   # true relationship: y = 2x + 1

w, b = 0.0, 0.0
best_loss = mse(y_data, [predict(x, w, b) for x in x_data])

for step in range(200):
    candidate_w = w + random.uniform(-0.1, 0.1)
    candidate_loss = mse(y_data, [predict(x, candidate_w, b) for x in x_data])
    if candidate_loss < best_loss:
        w, best_loss = candidate_w, candidate_loss   # keep the nudge only if it helped

print(w, best_loss)   # w ends up near 2.33, not 2.0, and the loss near 0.17 (see below)
```

This is mechanically 'learning': `w` is searched for, guided by whether each candidate reduces the loss. Note where it stops. Because `b` is never nudged and stays at 0, `w` cannot reach 2.0; the best slope with no intercept for these points is about 2.33, where the loss bottoms out near 0.17. The next example nudges both parameters. It is also an inefficient search, since it tries random directions and throws away every nudge that doesn't immediately help. Gradient descent replaces 'try a random direction and check' with 'use derivatives to compute the direction that reduces loss fastest, and go that way', which is far more efficient but solves the same problem this loop solves by brute force.

sections.heading: Loss vs. Evaluation Metric
sections.body:
The 'loss' a training run reports is not the number you'd give a stakeholder for 'how good is this model.' They serve different purposes and can move in different directions. Loss is chosen primarily to be mathematically convenient for optimization -- smooth and differentiable, so a gradient-based procedure can compute a useful direction to adjust `theta` in -- and it often isn't very human-interpretable on its own (a cross-entropy loss of 0.42 doesn't tell a product manager much of anything). An evaluation metric like accuracy, precision, or a business KPI, on the other hand, is chosen to be meaningful to humans and tied to what you care about, but is often *not* something gradient descent can optimize. Accuracy, for instance, has a derivative of zero almost everywhere: nudging a parameter slightly almost never flips a prediction from wrong to right, so gradient descent gets no useful signal.

The practical resolution is to optimize a smooth proxy (the loss) while judging success with a different, more meaningful metric -- and to watch for cases where they diverge. A model's cross-entropy loss can keep improving on paper while a metric that matters more for the actual business problem, like recall on a rare but important class, stagnates or even gets worse, especially under class imbalance. This gap between what training optimizes and what you care about is why the next module gives evaluation metrics a concept of their own: they answer different questions for different audiences, and neither substitutes for the other.

examples.title: Computing Mean Squared Error by Hand
examples.code:
y_true = [3, -0.5, 2, 7]
y_pred = [2.5, 0.0, 2, 8]

errors = [yt - yp for yt, yp in zip(y_true, y_pred)]
squared = [e ** 2 for e in errors]
mse_value = sum(squared) / len(squared)

print(errors)      # [0.5, -0.5, 0, -1]
print(squared)     # [0.25, 0.25, 0, 1]
print(mse_value)    # 0.375
examples.explanation: Squaring each error before averaging does two things. First, it makes every term non-negative, so a prediction that's too high and one that's too low both count as 'bad' rather than canceling out when summed. A raw, unsquared average of [0.5, -0.5, 0, -1] is -0.25, which suggests the errors mostly cancel. Second, squaring penalizes large errors disproportionately: an error of 2 contributes 4 to the sum, while two errors of 1 contribute 1 each (2 total). That makes MSE sensitive to outliers and occasional very bad predictions, which may or may not match what you want the model to prioritize.

examples.title: A Linear Model Is Literally a Function of Its Parameters
examples.code:
def predict(x, w, b):
    return w * x + b

x = 5

print(predict(x, w=0.0, b=0.0))     # 0.0
print(predict(x, w=2.0, b=1.0))     # 11.0
print(predict(x, w=-1.0, b=10.0))   # 5.0
examples.explanation: The function `predict` is never edited between these three calls. Every difference in output comes from changing `w` and `b`, the parameters. Training a model does not mean writing smarter code inside `predict`; for a fixed architecture, it means searching for better values of `w` and `b` to pass into the same function. Confusing 'a better model' with 'better code' is a common early misconception -- the architecture, the shape of `predict`, is a design decision made once; `theta` is what training solves for, over and over, automatically.

examples.title: A Toy Training Loop That Nudges Parameters to Reduce Loss
examples.explanation: Each quantity here has a job named earlier in this concept: `w` and `b` are `theta`; `predict` is the fixed function f(x; theta); `mse` is the loss function; and the `for` loop is the training step in its crudest form: propose a random change to theta, measure whether it reduces the loss, and keep it only if it does. Run enough times, `w` and `b` converge toward the true relationship (2 and 1) just by checking 'did this random nudge help?' and discarding the nudges that didn't. It's a legitimate, if inefficient, learning algorithm (random search against the loss). Keep this example in mind when the next module introduces gradient descent, which solves the same problem by computing a good direction instead of guessing one.

misconceptions.description: Training a model means writing or changing code (the algorithm); a smarter engineer who writes better code gets a smarter model.
misconceptions.clarification: For a fixed architecture, training does not modify any code at all -- it only searches for better numeric values of theta by minimizing loss on data. The 'learning' that happens is entirely about adjusting numbers, not logic. Code changes (architecture choices, feature choices, hyperparameters) matter, but they're a separate axis from what happens during a single training run, which is numerical search over parameters with the surrounding code held fixed.
misconceptions.fact: For a fixed architecture, training does not modify any code at all -- it only searches for better numeric values of theta by minimizing loss on data.

misconceptions.description: A model's loss during training and the accuracy (or other metric) reported to stakeholders are basically the same number, just measuring the same thing in different units.
misconceptions.clarification: Loss is an internal, usually-differentiable optimization target used purely to drive parameter updates, and it often isn't human-interpretable on its own: a cross-entropy value of 0.42 means little in isolation. The reported metric is chosen for human or business meaning and may not be directly optimized at all, since some meaningful metrics (like accuracy) aren't smooth enough for gradient-based optimization to use directly. A model can have steadily improving loss while an important metric like recall on a minority class stagnates or worsens, especially under class imbalance. Loss and the metric you report can diverge, not just differ in scale.
misconceptions.fact: Loss is an internal, usually-differentiable optimization target used purely to drive parameter updates, and it often isn't human-interpretable on its own: a cross-entropy value of 0.42 means little in isolation.

exercises.code:
import numpy as np

y_true = np.array([3, -0.5, 2, 7])
y_pred = np.array([2.5, 0.0, 2, 8])

errors = y_true - y_pred
squared = errors ** 2
mse = squared.mean()
print(mse)
hints: Compute the elementwise difference y_true - y_pred first, for all four positions.
Square each of those four differences -- notice the signs all disappear once you square.
Sum the four squared values and divide by 4 (the number of elements) to get the mean.
exercises.solutionExplanation: errors = [3-2.5, -0.5-0.0, 2-2, 7-8] = [0.5, -0.5, 0, -1]. Squaring gives [0.25, 0.25, 0, 1]. Summing gives 1.5, and dividing by 4 elements gives 0.375. Both negative errors (index 1 and index 3) contribute positively once squared, which is why squaring is used: a raw, unsquared average would let positive and negative errors partly cancel and understate how wrong the predictions are.

exercises.prompt: This loop is supposed to show the loss decreasing as w is nudged toward a better value, but the printed loss is identical on every step. Find and fix the bug.
hints: loss is computed from y_pred on every iteration -- when is y_pred actually recalculated relative to when w changes?
w is updated at the top of the loop body, but is anything downstream of w actually re-derived from its new value on each pass?
Move the line that computes y_pred to run fresh, using the current w and b, inside the loop, before computing loss.
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the original code, `y_pred` is computed once, before the loop starts, using w=0.0. Even though `w` is updated on every iteration, nothing recomputes `y_pred` from the new value, so `loss = mse(y, y_pred)` keeps reading the same stale list and the printed loss is identical on every step (41.000) while `w` visibly changes. The fix moves the `y_pred = [...]` line inside the loop, after `w` is updated, so the predictions, and the loss computed from them, reflect the current parameter value on every iteration. The bug pattern is common: updating a parameter but not recomputing everything downstream of it.

assessments.prompt: After a model has finished training and is deployed to serve predictions in production, which of the following is true of the predict/inference step?
options: It re-runs the full training loop on each incoming request to keep the model up to date.
It uses the already-learned parameters (theta) and only the input features X to produce a prediction; it does not require or use y at all.
It recomputes the loss function on every request and adjusts theta slightly before responding.
It still needs the true label y for each input, to check whether its own prediction was correct before returning it, and it discards that label afterward.
assessments.explanation: Inference means evaluating the fixed function f(x; theta) using the parameters training already produced. It consumes only X and has no need for y, since in a real deployment the point is predicting an outcome that isn't known yet. The “It still needs the true label y…” option describes something impossible in a real deployment (you don't have the label you're trying to predict). The “It re-runs the full training loop…” and “It recomputes the loss function on every…” options both describe training behavior, not inference -- re-running training or adjusting theta on every request would make the model a moving target and is not what a standard deployed predict step does.

assessments.prompt: For y_true = [3, -0.5, 2, 7] and y_pred = [2.5, 0.0, 2, 8], the raw (unsquared) errors are [0.5, -0.5, 0, -1]. Why does MSE square these errors before averaging instead of just averaging the raw errors directly?
options: Squaring makes every term non-negative so errors in opposite directions don't cancel out when summed, and it penalizes large errors disproportionately more than small ones.
Squaring is a mathematical requirement for computing the average of any list of numbers.
Squaring is done purely to make the printed numbers easier to read.
Squaring converts what would otherwise be a classification problem into a regression problem.
assessments.explanation: Squaring makes every term non-negative, so a raw unsquared average of [0.5, -0.5, 0, -1] would suggest the errors mostly cancel, and squaring also penalizes large errors much more heavily than small ones (an error of 2 contributes 4, while two errors of 1 contribute 1 each). The “Squaring is done purely to make…” option is a non-reason -- readability isn't why squaring is mathematically meaningful. The “Squaring converts what would otherwise…” option confuses loss mechanics with problem type, which is unrelated. The “Squaring is a mathematical requirement for computing…” option is false -- plain averages of unsquared numbers are computed constantly elsewhere without any such requirement.

assessments.prompt: The concept states that accuracy 'has a derivative of zero almost everywhere.' What practical consequence does this have for how models are actually trained?
options: Accuracy trains models faster than cross-entropy loss because there is less to compute per step.
Accuracy can only be computed once training has fully finished, never while it is in progress.
Gradient descent can't get a useful direction to adjust parameters from accuracy directly.
It means loss and accuracy are always numerically identical, just expressed on different scales.
assessments.explanation: Nudging a parameter slightly almost never flips a prediction from wrong to right, so accuracy gives gradient descent no useful signal. The practical resolution is to optimize a smooth, differentiable proxy loss while judging success with a more meaningful metric like accuracy, and to watch for cases where the two diverge. The “Accuracy trains models faster than cross-entropy loss…” option makes a speed claim that isn't true. The “Accuracy can only be computed once training…” option is false -- accuracy is commonly computed during training too, just not used to drive gradient updates. The “It means loss and accuracy are always…” option contradicts the point that loss and the reported metric can move in different directions.

assessments.prompt: A batch scoring pipeline joins in the true outcome column purely for later monitoring, after generating each prediction. According to the concept, what is the danger if that column is accidentally included as a model input at prediction time rather than kept separate?
options: It would only slow down inference slightly, due to the extra column being processed.
There is no danger, because the true outcome is always already known before a production prediction is made.
It would cause the serialized theta file to fail to load at all.

It reintroduces the data-leakage problem, now at serving time instead of training time: the model would be using a value that isn't genuinely available at the moment a real prediction is actually needed.
assessments.explanation: If a ground-truth column joined in for monitoring ever gets used as a feature during prediction rather than kept separate, you've reintroduced the data leakage problem from the earlier concept, now at serving time instead of training time, and this version is often harder to notice. The “It would only slow down inference slightly…” option trivializes a correctness bug as a performance issue. The “It would cause the serialized theta file…” option is a fabricated failure mode unrelated to leakage. The “There is no danger, because the true…” option inverts the point of inference: the outcome is what you don't yet know when a real prediction is needed.

assessments.prompt: Explain what it mechanically means for a model to 'learn,' in a way that would make sense to someone who has only ever thought of learning in the human sense. Be specific about the role of parameters and the loss function.
assessments.modelAnswer: A model is a function, f(x; theta), whose overall shape (linear, a stack of neural network layers) is fixed in advance by whoever designed it. theta is a set of plain numbers that function depends on, and 'learning' is an automated search for better values of those numbers. The search is guided by a loss function, which takes one prediction and the corresponding true label and compresses 'how wrong was this' into a single number -- small for a good prediction, larger for a bad one -- averaged across many training examples into an overall training objective. Training repeatedly looks at the current theta, computes how much loss it produces on the training data, and adjusts theta in whatever direction tends to make that loss smaller, over and over, until further adjustment stops helping much. Nothing in that process requires comprehension in a human sense; it is numerical optimization of a scalar function, and the 'intelligence' people attribute to a trained model is the result of that search having found parameter values that produce useful predictions. One more distinction: the loss minimized during training is not necessarily the metric you'd report as 'how good is this model'. Loss is chosen to be convenient to optimize, while a metric like accuracy is chosen to be meaningful to a person, and the two can diverge, which is why evaluation deserves separate treatment rather than being read off the training loss.
